lesson.menu_title: Under Fire — Three Hard Questions in a Row
lesson.menu_desc: Conceding without losing your position, naming a false premise, and giving the same answer again -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- Under Fire
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 11 -- Under Fire
lesson.grammar_point: contrast and concession for holding your position

listenings.text: When I put three hard questions together, I am not testing the answers. I already have the answers, or I would not be asking. What I am watching is the two seconds between them. Most candidates answer the first one well, and then something happens: they get faster, they get louder, or they start explaining the second one before I have finished asking it. That is the tell. The candidates who do this well are almost boring about it. They take the questions in my order, they concede what is true, they add the one thing that is also true, and then they stop and wait. Nobody has ever lost a process in my company for a decline in a margin. People lose it for what the decline does to them while they are sitting in front of me.

They asked me about the same number three times, in three different ways, and by the third time I was sure they thought I was lying. I was wrong about that. What they were doing was checking whether my answer would change under pressure, and it is a fair thing to check. The first time I gave the figure and the reason. The second time I gave exactly the same figure and the same reason, in almost the same words. The third time I said: it is the same answer, and I can send you the audited page this afternoon if that would help. The chairman laughed and moved on. I learned something that day. Under pressure, saying the same thing again, calmly, is stronger than finding a new way to say it.

extra_audio.text: Sandra asks three things at once: the margin, the eight months without a role, and never having worked abroad. Fernando says out loud that there are three parts, and takes them in her order. He concedes the fall in margin and contrasts it with the cash position. He accepts the second point as accurate, without turning it into an apology. He reframes the third one, because the premise is not quite right.
